190.title: The one who offers a leaf (9.11–9.25)
190.word: The one who offers a leaf
190.hook: a poor man brings the richest friend in the world a handful of flattened rice
190.howItsDone: In daily puja many Hindus offer flowers, tulsi or bilva leaves, fruit and water at the home shrine; Gita 9.26 is often recited to explain that what matters is the love, not the size of the offering.

segments.voice: Yesterday Krishna said, I will tell you the most secret, and the secret was wind resting in the sky. Your line was the secret. Today, what someone can bring to the one who holds everything. Day one hundred ninety.
screen: `"I WILL TELL YOU THE MOST SECRET" — THE SECRET.`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata Purana tells about Sudama, a poor Brahmin who had studied with Krishna as a boy. Years later Krishna is a king in a golden city, and Sudama's family has barely enough to eat. His wife begs him to go and visit his old friend. But what do you bring a king? Sudama borrows a few handfuls of flattened rice and ties them in a corner of his worn cloth. At the palace, Krishna runs to hug him, washes his feet, and then notices the little bundle he's trying to hide. What's that you've brought me?
screen: `A POOR MAN. A KING FOR A FRIEND.` → `A HANDFUL OF FLATTENED RICE.` → `WHAT'S THAT YOU'VE BROUGHT ME?`

segments.voice: In the story, Krishna takes the rice and eats it with delight, and he says a verse from the Gita. It's the verse that crowns today's reading: whoever offers me with love a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water, I accept that offering of love from the one whose heart is pure. That's Gita nine, twenty-six. Patram, pushpam, phalam, toyam. A leaf, a flower, a fruit, water. The four cheapest things in the world. Anyone can find them. The verses that lead up to it build the whole scene around that verse. Krishna has said fools look past him in human form. But great souls, verse fourteen says, are always singing about him, bowing, steady in their vows. He is the ritual and the offering, the fire and the ghee, verse sixteen. He is the father of the world, verse seventeen; the mother, the grandparent. He is the goal, the support, the lord, the witness, the home, the refuge, the friend. Then verse twenty-two, which many people know by heart: to those who worship me alone, always united with me, I bring what they lack and protect what they have. And so, when the Lord of everything gets to name what he wants, he names a leaf. Not because the gift is big, but because the love is real. The word the verse leans on is bhakti, devotion, love turned toward God. Sudama, the story says, walked home embarrassed he hadn't asked for anything, and found his hut had become a palace. That's today's word: the one who offers a leaf.
screen: `A HANDFUL OF RICE, EATEN WITH JOY.` · `A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT, WATER.` · `WHAT THEY LACK, I BRING.` · `NOT THE GIFT. THE LOVE.` · then, large: `THE ONE WHO OFFERS A LEAF.`

segments.voice: If you can, get something small before you sit: a glass of water, a leaf from outside, a flower, a piece of fruit. If not, picture one. Hold it in your open hands. Breathe. Think of what you'd want to offer with it: thanks, a worry, a person you love. If you pray, you can offer it to God, as the verse says. If not, simply hold it with care, as if it were a gift. The bell holds the time.
The one who offers a leaf. Gita nine, twenty-six: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water, offered with love, is accepted.
screen: `THE ONE WHO OFFERS A LEAF — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a leaf, a flower, water. Today, give one small thing with real love: a glass of water, a note, five minutes. Day one hundred ninety.

191.title: "Whatever you do, offer it" (9.26–9.28)
191.hook: one verse turns eating, giving and every ordinary chore into worship
191.howItsDone: Many Hindus offer food to God before eating (naivedya) and receive it back as prasad, and many try to dedicate their daily work as an offering in the spirit of Gita 9.27.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the one who offers a leaf, and Sudama's handful of rice. Your line was a leaf, a flower, water. Did you give one small thing with love? Today the offering gets bigger. Much bigger. Day one hundred ninety-one.

Walk into many Hindu kitchens before a meal and watch. Before anyone eats, a small portion is set aside, sometimes on a little plate in front of an image of Krishna or at the family shrine. A moment, maybe a verse. Then the food comes back to the table, and it isn't just lunch anymore. It's prasad, grace, a gift returned. Yesterday's verse was about a leaf. But a leaf is one thing. What about the rest of the day? The dishes, the email, the commute, the argument about whose turn it is to take out the trash? Today, one verse that takes all of it.
screen: `A PORTION SET ASIDE.` → `LUNCH BECOMES PRASAD.` → `WHAT ABOUT THE REST OF THE DAY?`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-seven: whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give, whatever discipline you practice, Arjuna, do it as an offering to me. In Sanskrit it's a list with a drumbeat: yat karoshi, whatever you do; yad ashnasi, whatever you eat; yaj juhoshi, whatever you offer into the fire; dadasi yat, whatever you give; yat tapasyasi, whatever effort you make. Five whatevers. And then one instruction: tat kurushva mad-arpanam, make it an offering to me. Look at the list. It starts with the most general thing, doing, and the second item is eating. Not meditating, not reading scripture. Eating. The Gita puts lunch right next to sacrifice. Yesterday Krishna asked for a leaf. Today he asks for the whole day. Not more stuff; more of your ordinary life, turned in a direction. And verse twenty-eight says what happens. You'll be freed from the bonds of action, with its good and bad fruits. With your mind set on this yoga of letting go, you'll be free, and you'll come to me. This is where chapter three's work without attachment and chapter four's sacrifice come together. The easiest way to stop clutching the fruit of an action is to give it away before you start. That's the word today: whatever you do. The shortest summary of the Gita some people know. Offer everything.
screen: `FIVE WHATEVERS.` · `EATING, RIGHT NEXT TO SACRIFICE.` · `NOT MORE STUFF. MORE OF YOUR DAY.` · `FREED FROM THE BONDS OF ACTION.` · then, large: `OFFER EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: Sit, and walk through the five whatevers for today. What will you do? Picture one task. What will you eat? Picture one meal. What will you give? One small thing. What effort will you make? One hard moment. For each one, take a breath and imagine handing it over before it happens: this is offered. If you pray, you can offer it to Krishna, as the verse says. The bell holds the time.
Whatever you do. Gita nine, twenty-seven: whatever you do, eat, offer, give or strive for, make it an offering.
Your line: offer everything. Pick one ordinary chore today, the dishes, the laundry, the drive, and do it as an offering from start to finish. Day one hundred ninety-one.

192.title: Even the worst (9.29–9.34)
192.hook: a highway robber becomes a poet; the Gita says the door was never locked
192.howItsDone: Many Hindus hold that devotion to God is open to everyone regardless of birth or past, and the story of Valmiki, the robber who became the poet of the Ramayana, is widely told to show that anyone can turn.

segments.voice: Yesterday: whatever you do, eat, give or strive for, make it an offering. Your line was offer everything. Did one chore become an offering? Day one hundred ninety-two, the end of chapter nine.

There's a story people tell about Valmiki, the poet of the Ramayana. Before he was a poet, the story goes, he was a highway robber, stopping travelers in the forest. One day he stopped a sage, who asked him a simple question: your family shares what you steal, but will they share the wrongs you did to get it? The robber went home and asked. They said no. He came back shaken, and the sage gave him the name of Rama to repeat. He sat so long repeating it that an anthill grew over him. And he came out a poet. Today, the Gita's word on people like that.
screen: `A ROBBER IN THE FOREST.` → `WILL YOUR FAMILY SHARE THE WRONG?` → `HE CAME OUT A POET.`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-nine: I am the same to all beings. No one is hateful to me, and no one is my favorite. But those who worship me with love are in me, and I am in them. Then verse thirty, the one that surprises people. Even if someone of very bad conduct worships me with undivided devotion, they should be considered good, because they've made the right resolve. Not good eventually. Good now, because of which way they've turned. Verse thirty-one: quickly they become righteous and reach lasting peace. And then Krishna tells Arjuna to say it out loud, to announce it: my devotee never perishes. Na me bhaktah pranashyati. Verse thirty-two widens the circle again. Those who take refuge in me, it says, even those whom the society of the time held low, women, merchants and farmers, laborers, reach the highest goal. It's a verse that names groups who were shut out of Vedic learning in its day, and readers today argue about its wording; some find it painful, some read it as those groups being singled out for welcome. Many readers hear in it a widening: doors that were closed, the Gita pushes open. Verse thirty-four, the last of the chapter, is the whole of it in a line: fix your mind on me, be devoted to me, offer to me, bow to me, and you'll come to me. That's today's word: even the worst. Nobody is too far gone to turn. No one is outside.
screen: `THE SAME TO ALL BEINGS.` · `EVEN THE WORST, TURNED, IS GOOD.` · `MY DEVOTEE NEVER PERISHES.` · `EVERY CLOSED DOOR, PUSHED OPEN.` · then, large: `NO ONE IS OUTSIDE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of someone you've written off. Maybe someone who hurt you, maybe a public figure, maybe a younger version of yourself. You don't have to excuse anything they did. Just hold them for a moment in the light of verse thirty: turning is always possible. Breathe in, and picture the door open. Breathe out, and let a little of the hardness go. The bell holds the time.
Even the worst. Gita nine, thirty: whoever turns with undivided devotion, whatever they've done, is to be counted good. No one is outside.
Your line: no one is outside. Today, notice when you're tempted to write someone off, and leave the door open a crack. Day one hundred ninety-two.

193.title: The source (10.1–10.11)
193.hook: even the gods don't know where Krishna comes from, because he's where they come from
193.tomorrow: Arjuna asks: how do I think of you? (10.12–10.18)
193.howItsDone: Many Hindus gather for satsang, sitting together to sing and talk about God, which verse 10.9 describes as devotees awakening one another; Gita 10.8 is a favorite verse on God as the source of all.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the end of chapter nine: even the worst, turned toward God, is counted good. Your line was no one is outside. Today, chapter ten opens. Day one hundred ninety-three.
screen: `EVEN THE WORST — NO ONE IS OUTSIDE.`

segments.voice: Stand at the mouth of a great river, where it meets the sea. It's a mile wide, brown and slow, carrying whole trees. Now follow it back. Up past the cities, past the villages, into the hills, until it's a stream you could step across, and then a trickle between two rocks, and then a single spring, water rising out of the ground. Everything downstream came from there. The Ganga's source is a glacier; people walk for days just to stand at it. Chapter ten of the Gita begins by walking everything back to its source.
screen: `A RIVER A MILE WIDE.` → `FOLLOW IT BACK.` → `A SINGLE SPRING.`

segments.voice: Krishna says he's going to speak again, because Arjuna delights in hearing. Then verse two: neither the gods nor the great sages know my origin, because I am the origin of the gods and the sages, in every way. You can't find the source of the source by going upstream. Then comes a list that's easy to rush past. Understanding, knowledge, clear sight. Patience, truth, self-control, calm. Pleasure and pain. Birth and death. Fear, and fearlessness. Nonviolence, evenness, contentment, discipline, generosity, fame and disgrace. All these different states of beings, verse five says, come from me alone. Notice that pain and fear are on the list. The Gita doesn't hand the hard things to someone else. Everything comes from the one source. Then verse eight, which many people know: I am the source of all; from me everything moves. Knowing this, the wise worship me, full of feeling. And verse nine, which is almost a picture of a good evening with friends: their minds on me, their lives given to me, they awaken one another, always talking about me, and they're content and full of joy. Bodhayantah parasparam: waking each other up. Then verse ten: to those always united with me, who worship with love, I give the yoga of understanding by which they come to me. And verse eleven: out of compassion for them, living in their hearts, I destroy the darkness born of ignorance with the shining lamp of knowledge. That's today's word: the source. Everything, even the hard things, flows from one spring.
screen: `THE ORIGIN OF THE GODS.` · `EVEN PAIN AND FEAR COME FROM ME.` · `WAKING EACH OTHER UP.` · `THE LAMP IN THE HEART.` · then, large: `I AM THE ORIGIN.`

segments.voice: Sit, and follow one thing back to its source. Start with the breath: where does it come from? The air in the room. Where does that come from? Plants, oceans, sky. Keep going back, one breath at a time, as far as you can. Then let the chain go and just rest, as if sitting beside a spring. If you pray, you can hold verse eight in mind: from you, everything moves. The bell holds the time.
The source. Gita ten, eight: Krishna says he is the origin of all, and from him everything moves.
Your line: I am the origin. Today, talk with one friend about something that matters, and see if you wake each other up a little. Day one hundred ninety-three.

194.title: Arjuna asks: how do I think of you? (10.12–10.18)
194.hook: Arjuna believes every word, and still asks the most practical question in the book
194.howItsDone: Many Hindus keep God in mind through particular forms and places: an image at the home shrine, a sacred river, a tree, a name repeated through the day, in the spirit of Arjuna's question in Gita 10.17.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the source. Your line was I am the origin: everything flows from one spring. Did you and a friend wake each other up a little? Day one hundred ninety-four.

Someone tells you something enormous. The ocean is two miles deep here. The universe is expanding. Your grandmother loved you more than anyone ever will. You believe it. You really do. But then you go and make a sandwich, and you have no idea how to hold that fact while spreading the mustard. Believing a thing and living with it are different skills. Today, Arjuna has just heard that Krishna is the source of everything. He believes it. And then he asks the most practical question in the Gita: okay, but how do I actually think of you?
screen: `SOMETHING ENORMOUS.` → `THEN YOU MAKE A SANDWICH.` → `HOW DO I THINK OF YOU?`

segments.voice: Verse twelve is Arjuna's confession of faith. You are the highest Brahman, the highest home, the highest purifier, the eternal divine person, the first god, unborn, all-pervading. And he adds: all the sages say so. Narada says it, Asita and Devala say it, Vyasa says it. And now you say it yourself. Verse fourteen: I accept everything you've told me as true. Neither the gods nor the demons know your full manifestation. Verse fifteen: only you know yourself, by yourself, highest person, source of beings, god of gods, lord of the world. That's a complete statement of belief. And then, verse seventeen. How shall I know you, master of yoga, by constant meditation? In which things, in which forms, should I think of you? It's a humble question, and a smart one. He's saying: I can't think about everything at once. Give me some handles. Where do I look? Verse sixteen already asked for it: tell me, without leaving anything out, your divine glories, vibhutis, the powers by which you fill all these worlds. And verse eighteen shows how he feels about it. Tell me again, in detail. I never get tired of hearing your words; they're like nectar. So chapter ten isn't a list for its own sake. It's an answer to a person who believes, and wants to know where to put their eyes on an ordinary day. Tomorrow comes the list. Today, the question. That's today's word: Arjuna asks. How to hold it.
screen: `YOU ARE THE HIGHEST BRAHMAN.` · `I ACCEPT IT ALL AS TRUE.` · `IN WHICH THINGS SHOULD I THINK OF YOU?` · `TELL ME AGAIN. IT'S NECTAR.` · then, large: `HOW TO HOLD IT.`

segments.voice: Sit, and ask Arjuna's question in your own way. Where, in your ordinary day, would it be easiest for you to notice something sacred, or something bigger than you? Maybe first light through a window. A child laughing. The first sip of tea. A piece of music. Let one answer come. Then spend the rest of the sit with it: picture it, feel it, let it be your handle. The bell holds the time.
Arjuna asks. After believing it all, he asks: in which things should I think of you? Give me something to hold.
Your line: how to hold it. Today, take the handle you found and look for it once, on purpose. Day one hundred ninety-four.

195.title: "I am the taste in water" (10.19–10.42)
195.hook: Krishna answers Arjuna with a list: the best of every kind of thing, and one entry nobody expects
195.howItsDone: Many Hindus honor the presences named in Gita chapter ten: they bathe in the Ganga, circle the sacred fig tree, chant Om and repeat a divine name (japa), seeing each as a glimpse of the divine.

segments.voice: Yesterday Arjuna asks: in which things should I think of you? Your line was how to hold it. Today, Krishna answers, with the longest list in the Gita. Day one hundred ninety-five.

Pour a glass of cold water on a hot day and take a long drink. That feeling, that exact clean taste of water when you're thirsty. Back in chapter seven, Krishna said: I am the taste in water. Not the water. The taste. The part you can't hold in your hand, that makes water water. Now, in chapter ten, Arjuna has asked where to look for him, and Krishna answers with a whole list built the same way. The best, the brightest, the deepest of every kind of thing. And somewhere in the middle, one entry that makes people stop and read it twice.
screen: `A LONG DRINK ON A HOT DAY.` → `NOT THE WATER. THE TASTE.` → `A LIST OF THE BEST OF EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: He begins at the center. Verse twenty: I am the self seated in the heart of all beings. I am their beginning, their middle and their end. Then the list. Among lights, I am the radiant sun. Among bodies of water, the ocean. Among words, the single syllable Om. Among offerings, the quiet repetition of a sacred name. Among mountains, the Himalaya. Among trees, the sacred fig. Among rivers, the Ganga. Among letters, the letter A, the first sound. Among seasons, spring, the one full of flowers. And, verse thirty-three, I am time that never runs out. Now the surprise. Verse thirty-six: I am the gambling of cheats. Wait, what? Commentators have long thought about that one. One reading: Krishna is naming whatever is the most intense of its kind, even the kind we wouldn't choose. Whatever grips hardest, there's a spark of his power in it. And then, verse thirty-seven, a wink: among the Pandavas, I am Arjuna. He's talking to himself. Verse forty-one gives the rule for the whole list: whatever is glorious, beautiful, or mighty, know that it springs from a spark of my splendor. And the last verse: but what do you need all this detail for, Arjuna? I hold up this entire universe with a single fragment of myself. So the list is a set of handles. The taste in water, the sun, the letter A. Things you meet every day. That's today's word: I am the taste in water. In everything.
screen: `THE SELF IN THE HEART OF ALL.` · `THE SUN, THE OCEAN, OM, THE GANGA.` · `EVEN THE GAMBLING OF CHEATS.` · `A SPARK OF MY SPLENDOR.` · then, large: `IN EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: If you can, pour a glass of water and take one slow sip. If not, remember the last time you drank when you were really thirsty. Stay with the taste: the cool, the clean, the relief. Then let your attention move to other simple things around you, the light, a sound, the air on your skin, and notice what's best in each one. If you pray, you can hold verse forty-one in mind: every glory is a spark. The bell holds the time.
I am the taste in water. Krishna's handles for the sacred: the best of each kind, every glory a spark of his splendor. In everything.
screen: `"I AM THE TASTE IN WATER" — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: in everything. Every time you drink water today, let the first sip be slow. Day one hundred ninety-five.

196.title: Arjuna asks to see (11.1–11.8)
196.hook: hearing isn't enough; Arjuna asks to see God's real form, and is told his eyes won't do
196.howItsDone: Many Hindus speak of darshan, seeing and being seen by the divine, when they visit a temple; chapter eleven, where Arjuna asks to see and is given a divine eye, is often read as the Gita's great darshan.

segments.voice: Yesterday: I am the taste in water, and a list of glories that ended in a single spark. Your line was in everything. Day one hundred ninety-six, the end of the week, and the start of chapter eleven.
screen: `"I AM THE TASTE IN WATER" — IN EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: Look back at this week. The one who offers a leaf. Whatever you do, offer it. Even the worst, and no one is outside. The source. Arjuna asking how to think of God. And the taste in water. A week of hearing. Arjuna has listened for ten chapters now. And there's a moment everyone knows, with a person you love who lives far away: the calls are wonderful, the letters are wonderful, and at some point you just say, I need to see you. That's where chapter eleven starts. The chapter that, centuries later, a physicist would quote in the New Mexico desert.
screen: `A WEEK OF HEARING.` → `I NEED TO SEE YOU.` → `CHAPTER ELEVEN.`

segments.voice: Verse one: out of kindness to me you've told me this highest secret about the self, and my confusion is gone. Verse two: I've heard in detail how beings come and go, and about your greatness that doesn't end. Verse three: it is just as you say. But I want to see it: your form as the Lord of all. And then, verse four, a lovely bit of humility: if you think I'm able to see it, master of yoga, then show me your imperishable self. If you think I'm able. He doesn't demand. He asks, and leaves room for no. Krishna says yes. Verse five: behold my forms, by hundreds and thousands, divine, of many colors and shapes. Verse six: see the gods of the sky and the storm, the twin healers, wonders no one has seen before. Verse seven: see the whole universe, moving and unmoving, gathered here in my body, and anything else you want to see. And then the catch, verse eight. But you can't see me with these eyes of yours. So I give you a divine eye. Divyam chakshuh. Behold my power. That's the key to the whole chapter. Seeing God isn't a matter of looking harder with ordinary eyes. The sight itself has to be given. In the Mahabharata, the narrator Sanjaya, telling all this to the blind king, has been given a divine eye too, so he can see the battlefield from the palace. That's how we get to watch. That's today's word: Arjuna asks to see. Show me.
screen: `MY CONFUSION IS GONE.` · `IF YOU THINK I'M ABLE, SHOW ME.` · `NOT WITH THESE EYES.` · `A DIVINE EYE, GIVEN.` · then, large: `SHOW ME.`

segments.voice: Sit, and close your eyes. For a moment, notice that everything you usually look at is gone, and something is still seeing: shapes, colors, the dark behind the lids. Rest in that. Then think of one thing, or one person, you'd like to see more truly than you do. Don't force anything. Just ask, in your own way, the way Arjuna did: if I'm able, show me. The bell holds the time.
Arjuna asks to see. After hearing, he asks for sight, and Krishna gives him a divine eye, because ordinary eyes can't see it.
Your line: show me. Today, look at one familiar person as if you were seeing them for the first time. Day one hundred ninety-six.
